historical_timeline.summary: Born in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands.
Regains the welterweight title; his opponent dies ten days later; the fight stays with him for life.
Retires after 112 professional bouts over nineteen years.
Badly beaten by a group of men after leaving a bar near Times Square; months in hospital.
A documentary about his life is released; a review reports short-term memory problems since the attack.
Pugilistic dementia, with full-time care, in a nursing home in Hempstead, New York.
Dies at 75 at an extended care facility in Hempstead.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: A neurocognitive disorder after repetitive head impacts and a later assault, with chronic PTSD, in a 67-year-old retired world champion boxer who comes with his care partner because of memory loss and confusion. The episode follows the 2003 Alzheimer's Association DETeCD-ADRD guideline (history from him and an informant, the MoCA and CDR, function, reversible causes, a medicine review, brain MRI and neuropsychological testing, disclosure and counseling) and shows how the NINDS 2000 criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome are research criteria, not a clinical diagnosis; how PTSD, depression and moral injury (guilt and self-blame after a fight in which his opponent died) are screened and treated under the VA/DoD 2002 PTSD guideline, with cognitive processing therapy adapted for memory problems, sertraline with sodium checks, and a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; why no cholinesterase inhibitor is used for mild cognitive impairment; falls; caregiver support; and advance care planning while he can take part fully. It respects the way he described his own life and sexuality, and makes no claim about his private health beyond the public record.

hpi.narrative: Emile Griffith returns two weeks after intake with his care partner and is seen the same day by Dr. Haddad-Lindgren at the memory clinic. He had a brain MRI this morning. His intake blood count, metabolic panel, B12 and TSH were normal. He started sertraline 25 mg each morning after intake; he had mild nausea for three days, which has gone, and no dizziness or bleeding. The nightmares about the title fight still come most nights. His first session of cognitive processing therapy is booked for next week. He missed the physical therapy evaluation booked last week: the card was mislaid and nobody called to remind him. He has had no falls and has not travelled alone since intake. He has had no thoughts of suicide.

assessment_plan.assessment: Dr. Haddad-Lindgren finds mild cognitive impairment (CDR 0.5) with a frontal-subcortical pattern: slowed thinking, poor set-shifting and retrieval that improves with cues. The MRI shows changes seen after traumatic brain injury (an old right frontal injury, microbleeds and a cavum septi pellucidi) with hippocampi normal for age. Repetitive head impacts over a long career and the severe assault thirteen years ago are the most likely causes; the NINDS criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, which are research criteria, are probably met; PTSD, depression and poor sleep add to the difficulty; Alzheimer's disease is less likely but not excluded

documentation.advance_care_planning: Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 30 minutes with him and his care partner, at his request, while he can take part fully. His capacity for these decisions was assessed: he understood what a health care agent does, explained in his own words why he chose his agent, and gave consistent answers. He signed a New York health care proxy naming his care partner as his health care agent, with a family member on the islands as the alternate; neither is named here. He said that what matters most is staying in his own home, being with the people he loves, being treated with respect, and not being a burden. If his memory one day fails to the point that he no longer knows the people close to him, he wants care focused on comfort, at home if possible, with no feeding tube and no machines to keep him alive; he wants his care partner and family to be able to visit and stay with him wherever he is. Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment were explained for a later stage and are not needed now. A financial power of attorney was discussed and he will arrange it. The plan will be revisited every year and at any change in his health.

referral.question: About a year of memory loss and confusion in a retired professional boxer of 67 with a long career, a severe assault with a head injury thirteen years ago, and chronic PTSD; MoCA 22. Please stage the impairment, weigh traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome against Alzheimer's disease, vascular disease and the effects of PTSD and depression, and advise on further testing, treatment and safety
referral.urgency: Routine; at the memory clinic two weeks from now, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit, with brain MRI that morning
referral.pertinent_history: Retired world champion boxer: 112 professional bouts over nineteen years, ending at 39. Thirteen years ago he was beaten by a group of men, one with a baseball bat, and spent several months in hospital, much of it in intensive care; short-term memory problems have been noticed since, worse over the past year: repeated stories and questions, losing the thread of conversations, mixing up days, two missed appointments, and once getting lost changing trains on a familiar route. Independent in personal care; reminders for appointments and help with bills (Functional Activities Questionnaire 6). MoCA 22 with losses in delayed recall (helped by cues), trail, cube, clock and letter fluency. Chronic PTSD diagnosed today: lifelong nightmares and distress about a title fight decades ago after which his opponent died, and about the assault; PC-PTSD-5 4, PCL-5 41; PHQ-9 9 with item 9 scored 0; safety assessment done with no ideation, intent or plan, and no firearms at home. Started today on sertraline 25 mg each morning, with cognitive processing therapy to begin; no other medicines and no sleep aids. Blood count, metabolic panel (sodium 140 mmol/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL), B12 418 pg/mL and TSH 2.1 normal. STOP-Bang 2. Timed Up and Go 13 seconds with one fall on ice last winter; physical therapy ordered. No tobacco; AUDIT-C 2. He does not drive. His care partner comes to visits

How likely are traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome as the cause, compared with Alzheimer's disease or vascular disease, and how much might PTSD, depression and sleep be adding?
Which further tests do you advise: neuropsychological testing, Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, or others?
Is any medicine for cognition indicated, and is sertraline a reasonable choice for his PTSD from a cognitive point of view?
What do you advise for safety when he travels, for falls, and for support for his care partner?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Griffith, 67, was seen with his care partner, who gave a consistent account with his permission. He boxed professionally for nineteen years, in 112 bouts, and cannot count the knockdowns or the times he was dazed. Thirteen years ago he was badly beaten and spent months in hospital; he and his care partner date the first memory lapses to that time, with a slow worsening over the past year rather than a sudden change. He now loses the thread of conversations, needs reminders, and finds names slow to come, though the names come with a hint. He has no headaches, seizures, tremor, change in walking beyond some unsteadiness, change in smell, dream enactment, hallucinations, impulsive behavior, rages or paranoia. He has nightmares about the title fight most nights and guilt about it, and sleeps about five hours. He started sertraline 25 mg two weeks ago, with nausea for three days that has passed.
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Fairbanks-Ochieng's intake note: MoCA 22, PHQ-9 9, PC-PTSD-5 4, PCL-5 41, Functional Activities Questionnaire 6, Timed Up and Go 13 seconds, normal blood count, metabolic panel, B12 and TSH; sodium 138 mmol/L today, two weeks into sertraline. Brain MRI this morning, reviewed with the images: mild generalized atrophy, more in the frontal lobes; hippocampi in the normal range for age (medial temporal atrophy score 1 on each side); a small old injury (encephalomalacia with hemosiderin) at the tip of the right frontal lobe; seven microbleeds at the gray-white junction of both frontal lobes; Fazekas 1 white matter change; a cavum septi pellucidi; no infarct, mass, subdural collection or hydrocephalus.

assessment.display: Mild cognitive impairment (CDR 0.5) of frontal-subcortical pattern
assessment.assessment: Slowed processing, poor set-shifting and retrieval that improves with cues, with preserved independence in daily life, fit mild cognitive impairment (mild neurocognitive disorder), not dementia.

assessment.display: Traumatic brain injury and traumatic encephalopathy syndrome
assessment.assessment: Repetitive head impacts over a long career and the severe assault are the most likely causes; the MRI shows an old right frontal injury, frontal microbleeds and a cavum septi pellucidi, and spares the hippocampi. He probably meets the NINDS 2000 criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (substantial exposure, a core cognitive impairment, a progressive course, not fully accounted for by another condition). These are research criteria: they cannot confirm chronic traumatic encephalopathy in life, they are not a clinical diagnosis, and they do not change treatment. The single severe injury makes it impossible to separate the two exposures.
Alzheimer's disease is less likely given the retrieval pattern and normal hippocampi, but co-pathology at 67 cannot be excluded. Vascular change is slight (Fazekas 1, no infarct).

assessment.display: Chronic PTSD, depressive symptoms and short sleep
assessment.assessment: These can impair attention and retrieval and are treatable; treating them is the best chance of improving his day-to-day thinking. Sertraline is a reasonable choice: it has no anticholinergic burden; sodium and falls need watching. Benzodiazepines, sedating sleep aids and anticholinergic drugs should be avoided.

recommendations: Neuropsychological testing in about three weeks to define the pattern, confirm the stage and give a baseline for follow-up

Alzheimer's disease biomarker testing (blood, CSF or amyloid PET) can be offered after the testing; it is optional if the result would not change his care, and with seven microbleeds he would not be a candidate for anti-amyloid antibodies whatever the result
No cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine: neither is shown to help mild cognitive impairment or traumatic brain injury

Continue sertraline and raise to 50 mg at six weeks if tolerated, with a sodium check two to four weeks after the change; continue cognitive processing therapy, adapted with written summaries, reminders and his care partner's help between sessions
Memory strategies: one calendar, phone reminders and a fixed routine; daily exercise, social activity and regular sleep
Safety: an address card, shared phone location and company on unfamiliar routes; shared oversight of bills; physical therapy for balance as already ordered
Support for his care partner: education, the Alzheimer's Association helpline and a caregiver class; the GUIDE model applies only if dementia develops
Advance care planning soon, while he can take part fully

Repeat cognitive testing yearly and neuropsychological testing in twelve to eighteen months, or sooner with change; return to the memory clinic for faster decline, parkinsonism, behavioral change or a fall with head injury
